entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11049"/><div sID="gen19897" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11049"/><hi type="bold">7. The morning--</hi>so Chaldean and Syriac versions (compare <reference osisRef="Joel.2.2">Joe 2:2</reference>). Ezekiel wishes to awaken them from their lethargy, whereby they were promising to themselves an uninterrupted night (<reference osisRef="1Thess.5.5-1Thess.5.7">1Th 5:5-7</reference>), as if they were never to be called to account [Calvin]. The expression, "morning," refers to the fact that this was the usual time for magistrates giving sentence against offenders (compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.10">Eze 7:10</reference>, below; <reference osisRef="Ps.101.8">Psa 101:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.21.12">Jr 21:12</reference>). Gesenius, less probably, translates, "the order of fate"; thy turn to be punished.<div eID="gen19897" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19898" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not the sounding again--</hi>not an empty echo, such as is produced by the reverberation of sounds in "the mountains," but a real cry of tumult is coming [Calvin]. Perhaps it alludes to the joyous cries of the grape-gatherers at vintage on the hills [Grotius], or of the idolaters in their dances on their festivals in honor of their false gods [Tirinus]. Havernick translates, "no brightness." <div eID="gen19898" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11051"/><div sID="gen19900" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11051"/><hi type="bold">10. rod ... blossomed, pride ... budded--</hi>The "rod" is the Chaldean Nebuchadnezzar, the instrument of God's vengeance (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.5">Is 10:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.51.20">Jr 51:20</reference>). The rod sprouting (as the word ought to be translated), &c., implies that God does not move precipitately, but in successive steps. He as it were has planted the ministers of His vengeance, and leaves them to grow till all is ripe for executing His purpose. "Pride" refers to the insolence of the Babylonian conqueror (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.31">Jr 50:31</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.50.32">32</reference>). The parallelism ("pride" answering to "rod") opposes Jerome's view, that "pride" refers to the Jews who despised God's threats; (also Calvin's, "though the rod grew in Chaldea, the root was with the Jews"). The "rod" cannot refer, as Grotius thought, to the tribe of Judah, for it evidently refers to the "smiteth" (<reference osisRef="Ezek.7.9">Eze 7:9</reference>) as the instrument of smiting. <div eID="gen19900" type="x-p"/>

Violence (that is, the violent foe) is risen up as a rod of (that is, to punish the Jews') wickedness (<reference osisRef="Zech.5.8">Zec 5:8</reference>).<div eID="gen19901" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19902" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">theirs--</hi>their possessions, or all that belongs to them, whether children or goods. entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11053"/><div sID="gen19904" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11053"/><hi type="bold">12. let not ... buyer rejoice--</hi>because he has bought an estate at a bargain price.<div eID="gen19904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19905" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">nor ... seller mourn--</hi>because he has had to sell his land at a sacrifice through poverty. The Chaldeans will be masters of the land, so that neither shall the buyer have any good of his purchase, nor the seller any loss; nor shall the latter (<reference osisRef="Ezek.7.13">Eze 7:13</reference>) return to his inheritance at the jubilee year (see <reference osisRef="Lev.25.13">Le 25:13</reference>). Spiritually this holds good now, seeing that "the time is short"; "they that rejoice should be as though they rejoiced not, and they that buy as though they possessed not": Paul (<reference osisRef="1Cor.7.30">1Co 7:30</reference>) seems to allude to Ezekiel here. <reference osisRef="Jer.32.15">Jr 32:15</reference>, 37, 43, seems to contradict Ezekiel here. But Ezekiel is speaking of the parents, and of the present; Jeremiah, of the children, and of the future. Jeremiah is addressing believers, that they should hope for a restoration; Ezekiel, the reprobate, who were excluded from hope of deliverance. <div eID="gen19905" type="x-p"/>

Calvin omits "is" and "which": "the vision touching the whole multitude shall not return" void (<reference osisRef="Isa.55.11">Is 55:11</reference>).<div eID="gen19908" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19909" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">neither shall any strengthen himself in the iniquity of his life--</hi>No hardening of one's self in iniquity will avail against God's threat of punishment. Fairbairn translates, "no one by his iniquity shall invigorate his life"; referring to the jubilee, which was regarded as a revivification of the whole commonwealth, when, its disorders being rectified, the body politic sprang up again into renewed life. That for which God thus provided by the institution of the jubilee and which is now to cease through the nation's iniquity, let none think to bring about by his iniquity. <div eID="gen19909" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11060"/><div sID="gen19917" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11060"/><hi type="bold">19. cast ... silver in ... streets--</hi>just retribution; they had abused their silver and gold by converting them into idols, "the stumbling-block of their iniquity" (<reference osisRef="Ezek.14.3">Eze 14:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.14.4">4</reference>, that is, an occasion of sinning); so these silver and gold idols, so far from "being able to deliver them in the day of the Lord's wrath" (see <reference osisRef="Prov.11.4">Pr 11:4</reference>), shall, in despair, be cast by them into the streets as a prey to the foe, by whom they shall be "removed" (Grotius translates as the Margin, "shall be despised as an unclean thing"); or rather, as suits the parallelism, "shall be put away from them" by the Jews [Calvin]. "They (the silver and gold) shall not satisfy their souls," that is, their cravings of appetite and other needs. <div eID="gen19917" type="x-p"/>

Compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.24.21">Eze 24:21</reference>: "My sanctuary, the excellency of your strength, the desire of your eyes."<div eID="gen19918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19919" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">images ... therein--</hi>namely, in the temple (<reference osisRef="Ezek.8.3-Ezek.8.17">Eze 8:3-17</reference>).<div eID="gen19919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19920" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">set it far from them--</hi>God had "set" the temple (their "beauty of ornament") "for His majesty"; but they had set up "abominations therein"; therefore God, in just retribution, "set it far from them," (that is, removed them far from it, or took it away from them [Vatablus]). entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11064"/><div sID="gen19923" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11064"/><hi type="bold">23. chain--</hi>symbol of the captivity (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.27.2">Jr 27:2</reference>). As they enchained the land with violence, so shall they be chained themselves. It was customary to lead away captives in a row with a chain passed from the neck of one to the other. Therefore translate as the Hebrew requires, "the chain," namely, that usually employed on such occasions. Calvin explains it, that the Jews should be dragged, whether they would or no, before God's tribunal to be tried as culprits in chains. The next words favor this: "bloody crimes," rather, "judgment of bloods," that is, with blood sheddings deserving the extreme judicial penalty. Compare <reference osisRef="Jer.51.9">Jr 51:9</reference>: "Her judgment reacheth unto heaven." <div eID="gen19923" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11065"/><div sID="gen19924" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11065"/><hi type="bold">24. worst of the heathen--</hi>literally, "wicked of the nations"; the giving up of Israel to their power will convince the Jews that this is a final overthrow.<div eID="gen19924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19925" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pomp of ... strong--</hi>the pride wherewith men "stiff of forehead" despise the prophet.<div eID="gen19925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19926" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">holy places--</hi>the sacred compartments of the temple (<reference osisRef="Ps.68.35">Psa 68:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.51.51">Jr 51:51</reference>) [Calvin]. God calls it "their holy places," because they had so defiled it that He regarded it no longer as His. However, as the defilement of the temple has already been mentioned (<reference osisRef="Ezek.7.20">Eze 7:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.22">22</reference>), and "their sacred places" are introduced as a new subject, it seems better to understand this of the places dedicated to their idols. As they defiled God's sanctuary, He will defile their self-constituted "sacred places." <div eID="gen19926" type="x-p"/>

Mischief ... upon ... mischief--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Deut.32.23">De 32:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.4.20">Jr 4:20</reference>). This is said because the Jews were apt to fancy, at every abatement of suffering, that their calamities were about to cease; but God will accumulate woe on woe.<div eID="gen19928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19929" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rumour--</hi>of the advance of the foe, and of his cruelty (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.6">Mt 24:6</reference>).<div eID="gen19929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19930" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seek a vision--</hi>to find some way of escape from their difficulties (<reference osisRef="Isa.26.9">Is 26:9</reference>). So Zedekiah consulted Jeremiah (<reference osisRef="Jer.37.17">Jr 37:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.38.14">38:14</reference>).<div eID="gen19930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19931" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">law shall perish--</hi>fulfilled (<reference osisRef="Ezek.20.1">Eze 20:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.3">3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.74.9">Psa 74:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.2.9">La 2:9</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Amos.8.11">Am 8:11</reference>); God will thus set aside the idle boast, "The law shall not perish from the priest" (<reference osisRef="Jer.18.18">Jr 18:18</reference>).<div eID="gen19931" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19932" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ancients--</hi>the ecclesiastical rulers of the people. <div eID="gen19932" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 26. Mischief ... upon ... mischief-- ( De 32:23 ; Jr 4:20 ). This is said because the Jews were apt to fancy, at every abatement of suffering, that their calamities were about to cease; but God will accumulate woe on woe. rumour-- of the advance of the foe, and of his cruelty ( Mt 24:6 ). seek a vision-- to find some way of escape from their difficulties ( Is 26:9 ). So Zedekiah consulted Jeremiah ( Jr 37:17 ; 38:14 ). law shall perish-- fulfilled ( Eze 20:1 , 3 ; Psa 74:9 ; La 2:9 ; compare Am 8:11 ); God will thus set aside the idle boast, "The law shall not perish from the priest" ( Jr 18:18 ). ancients-- the ecclesiastical rulers of the people.
